tldr: This survey asks how, and to what extent, AI shapes artistic creation, and it answers from two angles at once. On the theoretical side, it organizes the debates about AI Art into five open questions. On the technological side, it maps 78 AI Art projects into a design taxonomy of how AI is used in practice. Each perspective is used to test and inform the other.

facts.label: Technological lens
facts.value: Design taxonomy built from 78 AI Art projects

contributions: A survey of the main trends in the AI Art field, together with the literature selection methodology used to build the corpus.
A survey of the philosophical, ethical, and legal issues raised by AI Art, organized around five frequently debated questions.
A survey of the AI technologies currently used to create AI Art, summarized in a design taxonomy of creative stages, processes, and outcomes.
A correlation of the two perspectives that compares theoretical debates with current practice and points to future research directions.

sections.heading: Motivation
paragraphs: Computers have been part of art since the 1960s, but the paper argues that AI marks a line of demarcation: the machine no longer only executes the artist's instructions but appears to be creative on its own, raising new philosophical, ethical, and legal questions.

Existing surveys of AI Art focus mainly on technological achievements such as generative performance and controllability. Few address deeper issues such as creativity, authorship, and human–AI interaction. This survey pairs a theoretical review of those issues with a taxonomy of current practice, so that each can shed light on the other.

figures.caption: Research path of the survey: 143 papers and works are analyzed from a theoretical perspective (five issues) and a technological perspective (a design taxonomy), which inform each other.

sections.heading: Survey Method
paragraphs: The corpus combines reference-driven search, which expanded known "AI Art" references through cited and citing articles, with search-driven collection from relevant venues covering January 2015 to June 2025. Artworks by widely recognized Eastern and Western AI artists were added based on their participation in major exhibitions and public documents.

Papers were included if they examined AI-driven systems for creating, modifying, or editing artistic content, or the relationship between AI and artistic practice, especially human–AI interaction. From the resulting 143 items, 78 projects that practiced AI Art were coded qualitatively. Two authors reviewed each project independently, then refined the categories through iterative open coding.
bullets: Journals: TOCHI, TOG, TPAMI, TOMM, AI & Society, AI Magazine, and AIJ.
Conferences: CHI, UIST, CSCW, DIS, MM, UbiComp, SIGGRAPH, CVPR, AAAI, and ICCV.
Artists include Mario Klingemann, Sofia Crespo, Jake Elwes, Refik Anadol, Helena Sarin, Anna Ridler, Joy Buolamwini, Dabeiyuzhou (Lin Kunhao), and Ting Song.

sections.heading: Theoretical Threads
paragraphs: The theoretical survey frames the debate as five questions. Questions are more open to different perspectives than statements, and they give conceptual lenses for comparing studies. Most examples come from AI-generated visual art.
bullets: Creativity: can AI be "truly" creative? Using Margaret Boden's rephrasing of the Lovelace questions, the paper contrasts three views. The Strong View holds that AI can be creative, with positions from Boden, Terzidis, and Bown. The Weak View holds that AI only simulates creativity, with positions from Manovich, du Sautoy, Zylinska, and Crawford. The Emergent View uses computational systems to study and approach human-like creativity.

Attribution: who is the artist, the AI, the programmer, or the user? The sale of the GAN-generated portrait "Edmond de Bellamy" at Christie's in 2018 made the question concrete. With text-to-image systems, credit may be split between the users who write prompts and curate outputs and the developers who built the system.

Authorship: is AI implying the "death of the author"? Drawing on Barthes, Object-Oriented Ontology, and Benjamin's notion of aura, the paper discusses the idea that AI artworks possess an "objectivist autonomy", together with critiques based on technological and composite intentionality. It concludes that the question remains open.
Aesthetic value: what is the aesthetics of AI Art? The paper identifies three emerging trends: the aesthetics of the prompt, of the latent space, and of the data.

Ethics & law: biases built into training data are amplified by AI, while AI Art itself becomes a critical tool for exposing them. Legal disputes cover training on copyrighted images, mimicry of artists' styles, trademark confusion, and deepfakes that violate personality rights.

sections.heading: Aesthetics of the Latent Space
paragraphs: The paper notes that the aesthetics of AI Art is still taking shape and has been discussed mostly by artists and curators rather than scholars. It outlines three trends. In the aesthetics of the prompt, prompting is itself an art form: a prompt acts less like an instruction than a performative speech act that frames the latent space and shapes the outcome.

In the aesthetics of the latent space, artists such as Mario Klingemann and Refik Anadol describe their work as exploring the machine's "inner cosmos" or "digital subconscious". The latent space is both a poetic metaphor and a technical medium, a liminal "in-between" where hybrid forms can emerge beyond what the dataset contains. Jake Elwes, for example, uses it to reveal machine biases about gender and identity.

In the aesthetics of the data, the dataset is the raw material. Artists who work with large datasets tend to treat the latent space as the true medium and emphasize machine creativity. Artists who curate small, personal datasets, such as Anna Ridler, tend to engage critically with the data itself.

sections.heading: Design Taxonomy
paragraphs: The technological survey analyzes 78 AI artworks and tools and organizes them into three dimensions. It does not map point by point onto the theoretical questions. Instead, it provides complementary evidence of how AI actually participates in artistic creation.
bullets: Stage, viewed through the lens of artistic intention: Inspiring Intention, in which AI supports Ideation and Sketching, and Realizing Intention, in which AI supports Generation and Stylization.
Process, Input: Text, the most prevalent modality, plus Image, Speech, and Gesture.
Process, Model: GANs, VAEs, Diffusion Models, and Transformer-based Models.
Process, Creating Subject: Autonomous AI, Human-led, and Co-creation, distinguished by how much human control remains.
Outcome, Art Genre: Static Image, Video, Artifact, Installation, Creative Interface, and Performing Art.
Outcome, Scenario: Cultural Heritage, Education, Exhibition, and Commercial.

figures.caption: A taxonomy of how AI participates in artistic practice, organized by stage, process, and outcome. The illustrations were produced with ChatGPT 5 and edited by the authors.

Left: categorization of the 78 AI artworks and tools along the taxonomy. Right: example AI artworks, including works by Mario Klingemann, Sofia Crespo, Jake Elwes, Refik Anadol, Helena Sarin, and Anna Ridler.

sections.heading: Connecting Theory and Practice
paragraphs: Throughout the taxonomy, the survey links practice back to the theoretical debates. AI chatbots used for ideation can produce responses beyond the artist's original design, which the authors connect to Terzidis' notion of "unintentional intentionality". GAN artists often prefer small, curated datasets, which exemplifies the aesthetics of the data. The continuous, probabilistic latent spaces of VAEs give rise to the aesthetics of the latent space, while the noise-driven sampling of diffusion models turns controlled randomness into a source of variation and discovery. The autoregressive structure of Transformers grounds the aesthetics of the prompt.

The creating-subject dimension draws on Manovich's three forms of human control: data curation, algorithm selection, and outcome selection. Autonomous AI minimizes them, for example by letting the audience supply inputs or the system choose outputs. Human-led practice keeps all three, with AI as a tool. In co-creation the artist cedes some control and becomes a curator and interpreter of machine outputs. The survey notes that this paradigm is increasingly common, reflecting a trend toward greater autonomy in AI Art.

sections.heading: Limitations & Future Directions
paragraphs: The theoretical section is necessarily synthetic and simplifies some philosophical subtleties. The technological cases are illustrative rather than exhaustive, and the scope is limited to visual and performing arts. The authors propose two main research challenges.
bullets: Theoretical: evaluate the impact of increasingly accessible AI Art tools. They could democratize cultural production, but they could also homogenize artistic outputs.

Technological: integrate multimodal inputs so that users can express artistic intent through several channels. In the authors' framing, text offers semantic precision, sketches carry visual imagination, and gestures convey embodied expressivity.
